articles.title: Fine-Tuning Your Spring: Suspension Simplified by Mark Johnson

findings.claim: A rear that sinks deep into a long, loaded jump face lacks low-speed compression.
findings.fix: Add low-speed compression.

findings.claim: A rear that kicks on sharp holes exiting corners has too much high-speed compression.
findings.fix: Reduce high-speed compression; doing this together with adding LSC can cure both without upsetting balance.

findings.claim: A wallowing, rolling feel means the chassis is under-damped for the spring.
findings.fix: Add damping to make the bike predictable again.

findings.claim: For a stiffer overall feel, more preload stiffens evenly; a stiffer spring with less preload gives more support deep in the stroke.

principles: Springs respond to position, damping responds to shaft speed; tuning is the balance between the two.
A heavier spring with lighter damping can improve comfort and front feel, but past a point the bike starts to oscillate.
Preload shifts the whole spring force curve; spring rate changes its slope.
Rider feel can disagree with the numbers, so every change must be ridden and tested.

articles.title: Which Suspension Should You Use: Suspension Simplified by Mark Johnson

findings.claim: The 2024 KTM chassis draws common complaints about poor hold-up and hand feel, with a harsh spot in mid-stroke.
findings.fix: Either lift the bike above the harsh zone or let it pass through it smoothly.

findings.claim: The chassis tends to force a choice between handling precision and comfort.
Adding outer-chamber air to a coil cone-valve fork made it over-sprung and harsh, though bottoming improved.
findings.fix: Lighter mechanical spring plus reduced damping with the added air restored comfort and kept the hold-up; ranked best of three setups.

findings.claim: A valved stock WP fork and shock came a close second: better mid-corner and comfort, less precision.
findings.fix: Initial setting too soft; damping was firmed.

principles: Damping, spring rate and air pressure must be tuned together; changing one shifts the others' best value.

findings.claim: Stock AER air fork was stiff when new, harsh mid-stroke on braking bumps, and sat too low when air was reduced.

The rear does not follow the front well on corner entry.

articles.title: Setup Basics

findings.claim: Pre-ride checklist: align forks on the axle, set fork height, set air pressure each ride on air forks, set sag, set tire pressure, run terrain-appropriate tires.

principles: Correct springs for rider weight are the first and most important step; springs are not the tool for making the bike feel stiffer or softer.
Sag keeps the suspension working in the correct part of its stroke under the rider.
A revalve narrows the maker's broad compromise to one rider's use.

articles.title: Setting Sag

findings.claim: Wrong rear sag changes how weight transfers to the fork as well as how the shock works.

principles: Free (static) sag is a check that the correct spring rate is fitted, not a tuning target in itself.
Measure from solid metal points on the swingarm arc; points outside the arc can be off by up to 15 mm, and plastic flexes.
Measure with tank at least 3/4 full, rider in gear, neutral, brakes off, after bouncing to settle.

findings.claim: Harsh fork over bumps can come from trapped air in the fork legs.
findings.fix: Loosen bleed screws before each riding day.

findings.claim: Binding or stiff front can come from over-torqued triple-clamp bolts or overtightened holeshot rings on the fork leg.
findings.fix: Torque to OEM spec; loosen holeshot rings.

findings.claim: Rear binding or sag problems can come from factory-overtightened linkage bolts and thin bearing grease.
findings.fix: Grease steering, swingarm and linkage bearings on new bikes and re-torque.

findings.claim: Keep a log of date, track, conditions, feel, changes and final clicker, fork height and sag before calling a tuner.

articles.title: Suspension Simplified: Fundamentals of Setup by Mark Johnson

findings.claim: Front tucks in corners: too little fork compression support or too much weight on the front.
findings.fix: Add fork compression support / shift weight back.

findings.claim: Rear kicks sideways on braking bumps: rebound too slow to recover between hits.
findings.fix: Speed up rebound.

findings.claim: Rear kicks straight up: rebound too fast or spring over-preloaded.
findings.fix: Slow rebound or check spring/preload.

findings.claim: Head shake on throttle points to too little rear sag.
findings.fix: Increase sag.

findings.claim: Harsh on square edges may mean excessive high-speed compression.
findings.fix: Reduce HSC.

principles: More sag lowers the rear, slackens rake and lengthens wheelbase: more stable, slower to turn; less sag does the opposite and can bring head shake under braking.
If static sag is outside 30-40 mm, change the spring before touching clickers; ~20 mm static means too much preload and a stiffer spring is needed.
Low-speed compression controls pitch from braking, throttle and body movement and sets most of the rider's feel; too much gives harshness and lost traction.
High-speed compression controls impacts and mid-stroke support; too little lets the bike ride deep and deflect.
Rebound too slow packs and loses traction; too fast makes the chassis loose and kicky.
Hardpack: less LSC for grip; sand: more LSC and slower rebound; ruts: aim for balance and use fork height.
Worn oil, bushings and low nitrogen change damping; clickers cannot fix worn internals.
Change one thing at a time.

articles.title: Suspension Simplified: Common Mistakes

findings.claim: Rear kicking up over fast rollers usually means the shock is too soft and sinking too deep, not that rebound is too fast.
findings.fix: Add high-speed compression; slowing rebound instead can cause packing.

findings.claim: Dropping the fork in the clamps (e.g. 5 mm to 2.5 mm or flush) to stop a mid-corner tuck unweights the front: it pushes on entry then tucks at the apex.
findings.fix: Return fork height.

findings.claim: An under-damped fork feels harsh because the rider is using the deep, harsh end of the stroke.
findings.fix: Stiffen fork damping rather than raising the fork in the clamps.

findings.claim: Raising the fork in the clamps to reduce harshness costs stability and balance.

principles: Make small changes; if a change does nothing noticeable keep going in that direction until you feel it, and if it hurts, reverse it.
Harshness often means too soft (riding deep), not too stiff.

articles.title: We Ride Pre-Production All-New 2027 Honda CRF450R

findings.claim: Showa fork gets a new valve, 5.2 N/mm spring (from 5.0) for smoother low-speed damping; claims only.

Frame ~10% stiffer, more rake, longer wheelbase, pegs 5 mm rearward to load the shock; less pitching claimed.
More power lets Honda run taller ratios; gear-position-based ignition maps.
